cards.claim: Increasing batch size and decaying learning rate are quantitatively equivalent in effect on test accuracy
cards.conditions: SGD with momentum (m=0.9), Nesterov momentum (m=0.9), vanilla SGD, and Adam; CIFAR-10 wide ResNet-16-4; ghost batch size 128
cards.effect: Three training schedules (decaying LR, hybrid, increasing BS) produce nearly identical test accuracies and training curves over the same number of epochs
cards.evidence: Figures 2-4 show three near-identical training and test curves across multiple optimizers; text states equivalence holds across optimizers
cards.quote: When one decays the learning rate, one simultaneously decays the scale of random fluctuations in the SGD dynamics. Decaying the learning rate is simulated annealing. We propose an alternative procedure; instead of decaying the learning rate, we increase the batch size during training. This strategy achieves near-identical model performance on the test set with the same number of training epochs but significantly fewer parameter updates.

cards.claim: The noise scale (fluctuation magnitude) in SGD scales as η·B⁻¹, making batch size and learning rate inversely related in their effect on training dynamics
cards.conditions: SGD analysis in the framework of stochastic differential equations; interpreted as continuous optimization
cards.effect: Constant noise scale can be maintained either by decaying LR or increasing BS proportionally
cards.evidence: Mathematical analysis in Section 2 and 4; shows noise scale ∝ η/B for vanilla SGD and momentum methods
cards.quote: They showed that the mean and variance... They also proved that the 'noise scale' η/B, where η is the learning rate, the training set size and B the batch size. This noise scale controls the magnitude of the random fluctuations in the training dynamics... However we can achieve the same reduction in noise scale at constant learning rate by increasing the batch size.

cards.claim: When batch size is limited by hardware, one can achieve parameter-update efficiency gains by increasing batch size while keeping learning rate constant
cards.conditions: Wide ResNet on CIFAR-10, constant number of training epochs, batch size hardware limit = 8000 (half of training set)
cards.effect: Increasing BS from 128→640→3200 with constant LR=0.1 reduces parameter updates from 80000 to below 6500 while maintaining test accuracy 94.2-94.5%
cards.evidence: Section 5.2, Figure 5; training with increasing batch size schedule
cards.quote: Note that we only increase the batch size until it reaches B_max, after this point we achieve subsequent decays in noise scale by decreasing the learning rate.

cards.claim: Increasing initial learning rate and scaling batch size proportionally allows further reduction in parameter updates
cards.conditions: Wide ResNet on CIFAR-10, SGD momentum m=0.9, 90 epochs, scaling rule followed: initial LR η₀=0.5, initial BS B₀=640 (5× larger than baseline 0.1 and 128)
cards.effect: Reduces parameter updates from 29000 to 6500 while maintaining or improving test accuracy (94.4% → 94.5%), with no hyper-parameter tuning
cards.evidence: Section 5.2, Figure 5; 'Increased initial learning rate' schedule
cards.quote: 'Increased initial learning rate' also uses increasing batch sizes during training, but additionally uses an initial learning rate of 0.5 and an initial batch size of 640... 'Increased initial learning rate' requires under 6500 updates, reaching a final accuracy of 94.5%.

cards.claim: Increasing momentum coefficient while scaling batch size reduces parameter updates but slightly decreases test accuracy
cards.conditions: Wide ResNet on CIFAR-10, momentum coefficient increased from 0.9 to 0.98, initial LR=0.5, initial BS scaling to 3200 (25× baseline), 90 epochs
cards.effect: Test accuracy drops from 94.2% to 93.5% (0.7% loss) while reducing parameter updates from ~29000 to <2500 (>11× reduction)
cards.evidence: Section 5.2, Figure 5, and Table in text reporting median accuracies across 5 runs
cards.quote: Finally 'Increased momentum coefficient' requires less than 2500 parameter updates, but reaches a lower test accuracy of 93.3%. Across five additional training runs for each schedule, the median accuracies were 94.3%, 94.2%, 94.2% and 93.5% respectively.

cards.claim: The accumulation (momentum buffer) growth during early training creates a lag that becomes problematic at high momentum coefficients, requiring additional epochs to adapt
cards.conditions: Momentum m approaching 1.0; timescale for accumulation to reach steady state is ~1/(1-m) epochs
cards.effect: When momentum timescale becomes several epochs long, the accumulation cannot track loss landscape changes, particularly problematic at noise-scale decay points
cards.evidence: Section 4 analysis of momentum update equations; Appendix A
cards.quote: In Appendix A we analyze the growth of the accumulation at the start of training... We find that the accumulation grows in exponentially towards its steady state value over a 'timescale' of approximately 1/(1-m_t) training epochs... Once this timescale becomes several epochs long, the accumulation cannot adapt to changes in the loss landscape, impeding training.

cards.claim: Large batch training achieves similar test accuracy to small batch training when the same number of training epochs are used, even with batch sizes near the training set size
cards.conditions: Inception-ResNet-V2 on ImageNet, 90 epochs, decaying noise scale by factor of 10 at epochs 30/60/80; BS range 8192→81920, LR=3.0, m=0.9
cards.effect: Two runs of 'Increasing batch size' achieve final accuracies 78.1% and 76.8% vs 'Decaying LR' runs at 78.7% and 77.8%; difference within variance
cards.evidence: Section 5.3, Figure 6; two runs per schedule showing similar trajectories
cards.quote: The final accuracies of the two 'Decaying learning rate' runs are 78.7% and 77.8%, while the final accuracy of the two 'Increasing batch size' runs are 78.1% and 76.8%. Although there is a slight drop, the difference in final test accuracies is similar to the variance between training runs.

cards.claim: Increasing batch size dramatically reduces parameter updates per epoch, improving wall-clock training time with no loss of test accuracy
cards.conditions: ResNet-50 on ImageNet, 90 epochs, TPU pod (256 tensorcores); BS increased from 8192 to 16384 after epoch 30
cards.effect: Maintains 76.1% validation accuracy while reducing total training time from ~45 min to ~30 min; last 60 epochs + first 30 epochs both ~15 min each showing near-perfect scaling
cards.evidence: Section 5.4; actual wall-clock timing on TPU infrastructure
cards.quote: To utilise the full TPU pod, we then increase the batch size after the first 30 epochs to 16384 images, and achieve the same validation accuracy of 76.1% in under 30 minutes. The last 60 epochs and the first 30 epochs both take just under 15 minutes, demonstrating near-perfect scaling efficiency across the pod, such that the number of parameter updates provides a meaningful measure of the training time.

cards.claim: The linear scaling rule (proportional increase of learning rate with batch size) enables re-purposing existing schedules without hyper-parameter tuning
cards.conditions: SGD, momentum methods; when η ∝ B scaling is followed throughout training
cards.effect: Existing training schedules can be directly converted to large-batch schedules with equivalent accuracy
cards.evidence: Section 1 introduction and Section 5 experimental validation across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet
cards.quote: Crucially, our techniques allow us to repurpose existing training schedules for large batch training with no hyper-parameter tuning.

cards.claim: Higher initial learning rates reduce the margin before accuracy degradation: test accuracy falls for initial learning rates above ~0.4 on CIFAR-10 while holding batch size constant
cards.conditions: Wide ResNet on CIFAR-10, batch size constant at 128, momentum 0.9, varying initial LR from 0.1 to 3.2
cards.effect: Optimal initial LR near 0.4; accuracy loss for η₀ > 0.4 even without batch scaling
cards.evidence: Section 5.2, Appendix B; figure showing accuracy vs initial learning rate
cards.quote: We provide additional results in appendix B, varying the initial learning rate between 0.1 and 3.2 while holding the batch size constant. We find that the test accuracy falls for initial learning rates larger than 0.4.

cards.claim: SGD, Nesterov momentum, and Adam all exhibit the same equivalence between learning rate decay and batch size increase over fixed epoch budgets
cards.conditions: Three optimizers tested on CIFAR-10 wide ResNet-16-4; three schedules (decay LR, hybrid, increase BS); same number of epochs
cards.effect: All three optimizers show near-identical test accuracy curves across all three schedules
cards.evidence: Figures 3-4 showing SGD, Nesterov, and Adam results; text states 'all three curves closely track each other' even for Adam
cards.quote: We present additional results to establish that our proposal holds for a range of optimizers... Finally in figure 4b we repeat the experiment with Adam... Remarkably, even here the three curves closely track each other.
